g.passage: Nova had come up the mountain road above Marrakesh to repay an old loan, and the snow trapped both of them in Dalia's cabin for three days. On the first morning, Nova counted the money twice and set it on the table, but Dalia only pushed it aside and asked for help clearing the woodpile. Under the drift, the wind had uncovered a tin box Dalia had buried years earlier, holding every receipt from the loan, each one marked forgiven in faded pencil. Nova had spent a decade dreading this visit, rehearsing apologies on long bus rides. Now Dalia simply fed the stove and asked about Nova's work, as if no account had ever been open. Outside, the snow kept sliding off the cedar branches in soft, heavy sheets that hissed as they struck the ground.

g.passage: When Anselmo and Marisol were children, they rowed to the far end of the dock every evening and talked until the lake went black. Decades later, I watched them sit on that same dock without a word between them. Marisol had found, in her late mother's desk drawer, a letter showing that Anselmo's father had once paid the family's rent for a whole winter, and that no one had ever told her. She did not know whether to thank Anselmo or resent him for keeping quiet. Yet each morning she still carried two cups of coffee down the planks and set one beside him, and he still moved over to make room. Behind them, the fishing boats knocked gently against their moorings while gulls argued over the nets.

But after she fell asleep, he opened it again and, by the light of the corridor, began copying the crossed-out lines onto a clean page so he could read them without the ink scored through them. Esperanza listened, then spent the afternoon scrubbing the deck, coiling every line, and stacking her own crates out of sight in the hold. When Thiago asked why she was helping a sale that would put her ashore, she only said that she had seen him sell his father's boat the same way, and that he had not slept for a month afterward. He did the same every night after that, always waiting until I had signed. He had once told me that his uncle lost a job over a story no one bothered to check, and that he had never forgiven how quickly it spread. It said their cousin had fallen during a night patrol; the letter from another soldier said he had been carrying someone else. Bartolo looked past her at the harbor, where cranes turned slowly. He told her the report was accurate in every detail it chose to include. Fumiko felt something loosen in her chest, a small relief that he had not lied outright, but the heavier question stayed lodged there. Below them, a vendor wheeled a cart of carnations up the steep street, stopping every few meters to catch his breath.

g.passage: We waited at the mountain bus stop above Marseille, Remy and I, each holding a covered dish for the meal after the funeral. Mine was my grandmother's chickpea stew; his was the almond cake his father's family baked for every burial. Neither of us had seen the other in nine years. Remy joked that the two dishes would probably fight on the table, and I laughed harder than the joke deserved, glad for any sound at all. Still, I kept checking the lid on my pot, and he kept turning his cake so the dented side faced away from me. When the bus finally came around the bend, we both stepped forward at once and nearly collided, then stood aside for each other. Pine needles had collected in the gutter, and a thin wind pushed them in circles.

g.passage: Who keeps a broken jukebox in a diner for twelve years? One night Tommaso found him with the back panel open and a screwdriver in hand. Giacomo said he was only looking. g.passage: Promises outlive the people who make them. When I was seven, Kofi, my father's oldest friend, told me that the orchard behind his house outside Dakar would be mine to look after when I was tall enough to reach the mangoes. I measured myself against the lowest branch every visit. Then my family moved away, and Kofi grew too frail to walk the rows. Twenty years later, Abena, his daughter, walked me through the gate. The trees had gone wild, their branches knotted into one another. Abena said her father had called the orchard a letter he had never finished writing to me. I reached up and found that the lowest branch was now below my shoulder. A goat had wandered in through a gap in the fence and was nosing at the fallen fruit.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a letter he had never finished writing to me” most nearly suggests that the orchard
options: was described in letters Kofi sent to the narrator's family after they moved away.
contains a hidden message that Kofi left somewhere among the overgrown trees.
stood for an unfulfilled promise to the narrator that Kofi still meant to keep.
was a place Kofi visited to write while he was too frail to walk the rows.
g.explanation: 정답은 C이다. Kofi는 어린 화자에게 과수원을 맡기겠다고 약속했지만 가족의 이사와 그의 쇠약함 때문에 그 약속은 이루어지지 않았다. 따라서 '끝내지 못한 편지'라는 비유는 그가 여전히 지키고 싶었던 미완의 약속을 뜻한다. A, B, D는 모두 '편지'와 '쓰다'를 문자 그대로 해석한 오답이다.
